ingredients.h2: What is in the bottle, and what is not named
ingredients.intro: This is the one thing on the shelf whose label describes a ratio instead of a plant. Here is what the listing prints, and the three things it does not.

cards.alt: A glass dropper releasing a golden drop of oil into a shallow white dish of oil
cards.latin: Six parts omega 3 to one part omega 6
cards.p: That ratio is the only compositional figure on the label besides the tablespoon. It sets the two families of fatty acid against each other inside the bottle. It does not say which oil they were pressed or grown from, and the listing does not say elsewhere either. The drop in the picture is a generated scene rather than a photograph of ours.

cards.alt: A small amber bottle and a spoon of golden oil on linen, a generated scene
cards.p: The listing prints 9,000 mg of omega 3 in a tablespoon. That is a measured figure and it is printed, so it goes on the sheet. The listing then sets it against a recommended daily amount. Omega 3 does not carry a reference intake in the way iodine does, so this page prints the milligrams and leaves the percentage off.

cards.alt: Seaweed fronds in a ring of green nebula against a starfield
cards.p: A bottle named for DHA, whose one named constituent is alpha-linolenic acid, the omega 3 that comes out of plant seeds. The listing does not name the plant, does not name any other origin, and prints no DHA figure of its own. The picture here is the painted illustration for the sea moss shelf, where the bottle sits because it goes into the gel. It is not a statement about the source, and neither is the shelf.

Store in the fridge is the one storage instruction on this listing, and it is the one line that separates this bottle from every capsule on the site. The photograph is of jars of gel on the fridge shelf in the shop rather than of bottles of the oil.

rows: An oil blended at six parts omega 3 to one part omega 6. The listing prints that ratio and prints no source.
Not printed. The listing names alpha-linolenic acid, which is the omega 3 of plant seed oils, and it does not name the plant. We are not going to name one on its behalf.
No figure. The bottle is called Omega DHA Oil and the listing prints no DHA quantity anywhere on it.

One tablespoon a day, as printed. A tablespoon is 15 ml.

Chondrus Crispus Sea Moss Gel, as the third of three declared ingredients. How much of it goes into a jar is not printed, so a spoonful of that gel is not a way of measuring this oil.

Not for children. If you take warfarin or any other anticoagulant, ask your GP or pharmacist before you start. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, ask your midwife or pharmacist. If you avoid particular oils, ring the shop before you buy, because the label will not tell you what this is.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: The ratio, the tablespoon, the milligrams of omega 3 and the fridge are printed on the listing and all four are on the sheet. The source of the oil, the volume of the bottle and any DHA figure are not printed, and they are named as missing rather than filled in. What an omega oil does in a person is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not here.

reiss.label: Reiss's turn
reiss.h2: A bottle named for a figure it does not print
paras: This one is called Omega DHA Oil. The listing prints no DHA quantity. What it does print is alpha-linolenic acid, which is the omega 3 you get out of plant seeds, a total of nine grams of omega 3 in a tablespoon, and a ratio of six to one. Those are real numbers and they are all on the sheet. The name is doing something the numbers underneath it are not doing, and I would rather say that on our own page than have you work it out afterwards.

The second gap is the source. No plant is named on this label and no other origin is named either. That is why this is the one thing in the shop without a vegan mark on its sheet: I do not know what is in the bottle well enough to put a mark on it, and a mark I cannot evidence is worse than an empty line. It is also why the allergen row says nothing useful. If that matters to you, ring the counter and I will tell you exactly what the supplier has told me, which at the time of writing is not enough.

The third is the bottle itself. A month at a tablespoon a day comes out at about four hundred and fifty millilitres, and I am not printing four fifty, because nobody has printed it to me. All three of those are label problems rather than product problems, and all three are on the reprint list.
reiss.pull: The name is doing something the numbers underneath it are not doing.
